blocks.text: Our first true eval for continual learning.

Imagine every time you had a new experience, you wrote it down. Now imagine that you wanted to train a LLM on all of your experiences, so the model actually knows you in a deep way. In our new paper, we tested exactly this for a fictional character named “Elias Zhang.”

Doing this requires two things: 1) continual learning, since experiences arrive every day and the model must learn new ones without forgetting past experiences, and 2) knowledge injection: turning a description of an experience into knowledge the model can actually use.

If achieved, this of course has applications in AI personalization.  Our paper Complementary Learning System for Continual Episodic Memory in LLMs explores both. We originally approached this as a way to model human memory using an LLM, but several results have practical implications:
We provide the first true benchmark of in-the-weights continual learning
All techniques exhibit severe forgetting (LoRA, regularization, distillation)
We find memorization capacity to be 2 parameters per token
We find substantial gains in accuracy by changing how new knowledge is presented during training.
We propose a fast/slow memory system that encodes new memories and later merges to base model via consolidation/sleep.
0) Background

Currently there are 3 ways of doing continual learning in LLMs: 1) in the context-window, 2)  harness engineering, or 3) in the weights. The first works well but faces cost, context rot, and a finite window. The second is a good approach and a lot of new research is going into it. But the third is how humans do it (synaptic changes), and it's the only one that leaves an imprint on the underlying model, and is thus our focus.
1) Our first human-like CL Benchmark

Via synthetic data, we created 1000 experiences of a fictional character named Elias Zhang, chronologically following his life from age 15 to 64 (1960–2009). We then train on these experiences, one at a time. I want to emphasize how non-standard it is.

Training datasets are usually tens of thousands of examples, each example thousands of tokens. We are training on 1 example, about a paragraph long (100 tokens). Somehow the model must get this information into the weights. Literally batch size 1, each experience seen once, no replay. This is continual learning the way humans experience it.
Here's an example:

"On a tense Tuesday night in early November 1960, my father turned up the crackling AM radio behind the cash register in our Chinatown restaurant so we could hear the Kennedy–Nixon election returns. Between refilling teacups and clearing plates, I listened to the announcer's excited voice and wondered if anything would change for people like us."
We call this the fictional character dataset. We have an accompanying QA test-set, which tests if the model understood the information, ie

Q: Where in the restaurant was the AM radio your father turned up on election night in November 1960?
 A: Behind the cash register.
The second metric we have is reconstruction. Each experience has a title/theme, and during evaluation the model is tasked to reconstruct all details of the events given the theme.
Sort of like when a friend says “remember that time when….” and gives a small description of what was a larger event.
We have a second dataset, the Wiki dataset: 1,000 Wikipedia paragraphs published after the models' training cutoff.
The models, before trained on any of the datasets, achieve ~0% QA accuracy, meaning our datasets are entirely uncontaminated.
2) Results

Across both datasets, both metrics, and multiple models, there is extreme catastrophic forgetting. LoRA, which was reported to mitigate forgetting (Biderman et al.), even the recent hype for on-policy distillation to enable continual learning, and regularization methods (L2, or elastic-weight consolidation) all fail.
3) How many parameters does a memory need? 2 per token.
Before tackling interference, we ask a narrower question: how few new parameters are enough to store one episode faithfully?

We start with a rank-2 LoRA adapter on a single weight matrix. Then we restrict it to randomly selected subsets of input and output neurons. We call this masked LoRA. With m selected neurons on each side, the adapter has just 4m trainable parameters.
We then find the minimal necessary parameters for the model to reconstruct its training sample exactly for a single experience.
We sweep layers and weight matrices (attention + MLP), and find that about 2 parameters per token are necessary when taking the best combination (layer 10 down projection matrix).

For scale: at that rate, all 1,000 Wiki episodes fit in 197K adapter parameters. That's 0.0025% of an 8B model, 0.39 MB in fp16. Note however, that this is to memorize the experiences, not generalizing to QA performance.
4) Best Data Augmentation Techniques

We find that these very parameter-efficient adapters work perfectly on reconstruction, but do not generalize to QA ability. So now the knowledge injection problem. Given a single new experience (N=1), what do you do to the paragraph so the model can later answer questions about it directly?
The ladder is
train naively on the passage (ie continued pre-training)
+ train on paraphrases (LLM rewrites as alternative targets)
+ knowledge-instruction (Ovadia et al.): break the passage into declarative facts, up to 50 per episode, and train on the facts
masked reconstruction (Pan, Hahami et al): replace 45% of the tokens with a mask token and train the model to recover the original sample.

Thus, a prractical takeaway is: if you're injecting novel knowledge by fine-tuning, use extracted facts and/or masked reconstruction/ a denoising objective. Plain SFT on the text is the worst thing you can do.
5) Fast memories, slow integration
My bet is that gating will play an important role in continual learning: selecting which adapters should activate upon an input.

The inspiration comes from neuroscience’s complementary learning systems theory. The hippocampus rapidly encodes relatively separated traces of new experiences, while the neocortex learns more slowly. Replay (e.g. during sleep) helps consolidate experiences into longer-term knowledge.
We implement a functional version of that organization with LoRA:
The pretrained base model supplies stable background knowledge.
Each episode receives its own small adapter.
An embedding-based gate selects the adapter most relevant to the incoming cue.

As per the results of our paper, this architecture helps mitigate forgetting since interference is prevented by construction by storing experiences in seperate adapters. Now comes the part where we need to merge these experiences (that are in the hippocampus / LoRAs) to the base weights (the cortex).
Now comes “sleep.”

We implemented consolidation: batch-replay the stored episodes into the base weights (a rank-2048 LoRA merged in, all MLP layers), then discard the adapters. Cued with an episode's embedding, the consolidated model reconstructs all 1,000 episodes near-perfectly with no adapter attached, and keeps 94–95% of its general capability.

We can repeat this process:  rapidly encode new memories in ultra-paramter efficient (2 params per token) LoRAs capable of reconstructing the data sample. Then during "sleep," reconstruct the experiences and consolidate them back into the base weights via the data augmentation techniques in section 4.  This gives strong reconstruction and QA ability, with only a very slight degradation of base capabilities.
We hope this work builds on other work towards adaptable AI.
